reason: Host tools behind one queued service give the same result in every deployment, which a shell command under a sandbox did not. The tool contract carries over unchanged; the Go host cannot load the Node LibreOffice Kit module in-process, so the document area must choose how the engine is hosted (a supervised helper process is the likely form).
summary: Office rendering, conversion and recalculation are three host tools (`office_render`, `office_convert`, `office_recalculate`) that appear only in sessions that load an Office skill. They call the Office kit service inside the host, so they share the queue, limits and cache of Office previews instead of running a LibreOffice command line through the sandboxed shell.

reason: Models copy 36-character ids badly and pay tokens for them in every listing; a short name fixes a model-facing problem that does not depend on the host language. The synchronous reservation at admission maps to a mutex-guarded set in Go.
summary: Each child agent gets a short name (1 to 32 lower-case letters, digits or hyphens, default `agent-N`) that is unique among its creator's children and stored in the creator's catalog entry. The session id stays the only execution identity; a name is a model-facing reference that tools resolve to it.

reason: The need (an extension decorates or wraps a region it does not own) stands, but a React higher-order component has no meaning in server-rendered HTML. The Go UI needs a template-level wrapper extension point with the same ordering and shadowing rules.
summary: The client slot system gains a fifth kind, `hoc`, that lets a plugin wrap the owner's content in ordered layers and so become an ancestor of that content, which the sibling-only slot kinds cannot do.

reason: Separating the workspace root from a model-moved cursor is what lets file views, change summaries and write boundaries follow the checkout and nothing else. The Go design can start with this model and has no stored `working-directory/change` events to ignore.
summary: A session works in one directory that only host operations move. The model-facing `working_directory` tool and the `cwd` parameter of the delegation tools are removed; `header.cwd` stays the immutable original project, and a new `workspace-root/change` event records a changed checkout such as an entered worktree.

reason: This is an npm package naming rule enforced by an upstream repository script. Go packages are identified by import path inside one module, and moving a package is a compiler-checked refactor.
summary: New experimental packages are published as `@deepseek-ai/dsh-<name>` without an `experimental` prefix, so promoting one to a product group does not rename it; a constraints script keeps the list of legacy prefixed packages shrinking.

reason: The goal (a stylesheet reaches the page once and its lifetime belongs to the document, not to script loading) stands. The Go host serves stylesheets as static assets linked from templates, so there are no client module manifests to carry them.
summary: A client module artifact carries optional metadata that describes its stylesheets by path. The module system owns JavaScript identity, and the renderer installs, de-duplicates, updates and removes stylesheets in the main document; script loading no longer injects CSS.

reason: The split is an interface design that Go expresses directly with embedded interfaces, and it keeps window behaviour from depending on an application-level capability check.
summary: Computer Use (CUA, the capability that drives desktop applications) exposes one shared surface for operations common to applications and windows, with application-only and window-only operations added on top. Static provider capabilities are fixed at install and kept apart from runtime permissions, and keyboard input separates a key from its modifiers (`pressKey`) and from single key-down or key-up events (`sendKeyEvent`).

reason: The goal (every expected failure carries a stable code the tool registry can record, without pulling in the LLM runtime) stands. Go has no class-identity problem: a small error interface in a leaf package, checked with `errors.As`, gives the same result and needs no re-export.
summary: The `HarnessError` base class lives in a package with no dependencies, because the tool registry records an error's name and code only when the thrown value is an instance of that one class. `dsh-llm` re-exports it so both import paths name one constructor.

reason: Per-language fence rendering by extensions stays a requirement (diagrams, charts, previews). In the Go UI the Markdown renderer runs on the host, so the extension point is a host-side registry of fence renderers keyed by language, not a React slot.
summary: Chat hands each Markdown fenced code block to a delegate, which dispatches it by language through a keyed `hoc` slot, so a plugin can register, replace or decorate the rendering of one language.

reason: The host already decides everything the page shows, which is exactly the shape server-rendered HTML wants, and registration that returns a disposer maps onto a cordis service. Only the browser half changes form, to a template, under DH-ADR-3.
summary: One host registry (`ctx.connectorAccounts`) holds every connector account, whether it lives in a vendor command-line tool or in an OAuth grant held by the MCP manager. The host decides phase, status text, buttons and confirmations; the browser only displays them and opens the authorization page.

reason: Keeping credential knowledge out of transports and route handlers is a security boundary, not a JavaScript artefact. In Go the provider is an interface registered with an authentication service and the Peer travels in the request context.
summary: Shows how a credential plugin plugs in: it uses the `connection` service to create a Peer (the authenticated caller identity) and the nested `connection.authentication` service to register a verifier. Route owners and transports receive the selected Peer and never handle tokens.

reason: The host serves tool-capable operations, so a reachable address must never establish identity, and one authorization model for browser token, desktop and remote pairing is needed whatever the UI technology. Server-rendered pages and server-sent event streams pass through the same admission.
summary: Authentication is an independent service that tries registered credential Providers in registration order and accepts the first live Peer. If all refuse the answer is 401, and if a verifier failed it is 503; the web server enforces route admission, and gateway and remote access authorize operations from the Peer.

reason: One adapter in place of per-connector account code removes the 23 strings and the state handling that every connector repeated. The adapter is plain host logic over two services.
summary: An adapter service (`ctx.mcpAccounts`) registers each OAuth MCP server as a connector account under the key `mcp:<server>`, reads its status from the MCP manager and maps the manager's states to the shared connect, sign-out and retry operations.

reason: Serving a capability over MCP through the same tool pipeline keeps consent, cancellation and state ownership in one place. In Go the profile is a configuration of compiled-in components (DH-ADR-4), so the optional-bundle packaging part of the note does not carry over.
summary: Computer Use is offered to other agent harnesses as an MCP stdio server that runs inside a standalone `cua-mcp` profile. One stdio connection owns one Agent, created before the transport opens and disposed at end of input, and each call runs through the ordinary tool pipeline with no model step.

reason: A per-call override under a provider-enforced ceiling is a language-neutral way to bound work and output.
summary: An accessibility-tree read takes `maxElements` and `maxDepth` from the request when given and from provider configuration otherwise, so a caller can go deeper for one read without raising the defaults for every later read. The native provider still enforces its own ceilings.

reason: One tool form per agent and scope-owned registration follow the cordis ownership model the Go port already has. It depends on the Go design keeping a program runtime (see the PTC notes); that runtime is a separate process upstream as well.
summary: Agents on the PTC preset get the raw `cua` tool; every other agent gets `cua_run_code`, a program tool built from the shared program-tool factory with one isolated, state-retaining runtime per agent. Registration is by agent scope, so enabling or disabling the provider affects existing and later agents without editing presets.

reason: Explicit output selection is a model-facing contract that keeps intermediate tool results out of the context window. The formatting runs inside the JavaScript program runtime, which stays a separate process, so the Go host only transports the selected output.
summary: A `run_code` program chooses what the model sees by calling `inspect(...values)`; text, objects and images appear in one ordered output. The final expression or return value is discarded, so incidental data never reaches the model's context.

reason: Models redeclare names across calls whatever the host is written in, so the behaviour must hold. The evaluator is JavaScript that runs inside the program runtime process, not in the host, so it can be carried inside that runtime helper for as long as programs stay TypeScript.
summary: Retained `run_code` state moves from Node's global REPL scope to a scoped evaluator (a scope-chain kernel plus an evaluator), so a later program may declare a `const`, `let` or `class` name again instead of failing before any statement runs.

reason: Central ownership of the credential choice removes helper code that each DeepSeek consumer copied, and never handing out the raw secret is a security property worth keeping. Context cancellation replaces the abort signal in Go.
summary: One service (`ctx.deepseekAuth`) decides which credential a DeepSeek request uses, an API key or the account sign-in. A consumer describes the request (accepted kinds, billing, model route, destination) and receives ready headers plus a revocation signal; it never sees a bare credential value.

reason: Without it the default Computer Use configuration has no effect in headless and SDK hosts. Optional dependencies that re-evaluate on load and unload are a cordis feature the Go port has.
summary: Agents that join no preset (SDK, headless and ACP applications) also receive `cua_run_code`; only agents on the configured preset receive raw `cua`. The preset registry becomes an optional dependency, and the provider recomputes each live agent's tool form when the registry loads or unloads.

reason: Cancelling on log overflow leaves the caller unable to tell which external actions ran, and a retry repeats them. Truncate-and-continue is the safe rule for any program that has side effects.
summary: When a program's captured output exceeds its budget, the runtime keeps an ordered prefix, drops the rest and sets `outputTruncated`; it does not cancel the program or discard retained variables. A truncated failure keeps its failure kind.

reason: The goal (a configuration change shows in an open page without a reload, and secrets never leave the host) stands. With server-rendered HTML there is no browser plugin to configure: the host renders from current configuration and pushes re-rendered fragments over server-sent events.
summary: Browser plugins receive the volatile (live-updatable) fields of their host configuration, pushed on change without remounting the plugin. Secret positions are removed on the host and never sent, and equal values cause no update.

reason: The goal (switching back to a recent session is instant, and idle sessions do not pay for derived work) stands. The Go UI keeps session state on the host, so the equivalent is a host-side cache of rendered conversation state with an eviction rule, not browser object retention.
summary: A client Session reference states what it keeps alive: the event connection, and named facets of derived computation. Recently viewed sessions stay retained so returning to one does not pull history again, while expensive derived work runs only for references that ask for it.

reason: This is upstream npm release tooling and CI hygiene. A Go release produces binaries and has no packed-install verifier.
summary: The release script that verifies a packed npm install passes its own `--cache` directory to npm and deletes it together with the temporary consumer, so repeated release rehearsals do not fill the shared runner's disk.

reason: Authentication is the identity boundary and locality is not, so a remote user must not lose preferences on reload. Host-stored preferences are also the natural model for a server-rendered UI.
summary: Every authenticated browser reads and writes the same host settings store; whether the page is loopback or remote no longer selects a different store. Only the Open configuration file button is hidden on non-loopback pages, as a presentation choice.

reason: The symptom comes from a browser-side mirror racing the host's list. With a server-rendered list the host is the only source, so the Go design must instead mark a session as no longer blank at prompt acceptance, before the turn starts.
summary: The client's session manager remembers which sessions have had a prompt accepted, so a later list refresh or reconnect that still reports the session as blank does not turn its row back into New Session.

reason: The goal (opening an old session causes one cold read, not several competing ones) stands. Go can compare the service instance directly and collapse concurrent opens into one in-flight read, and under DH-ADR-3 the host orders the auxiliary reads itself.
summary: The prepared-observation cache identifies its producer by a per-instance identity token plus the log revision, so access through a proxy no longer invalidates it falsely. Auxiliary client requests (skills, commands, goals, references) wait until the conversation's initial open succeeds before they touch a cold log.

reason: Models fill in irrelevant optional fields; rejecting those calls costs a retry and protects nothing. The rule is model-facing and applies to every provider, so the Go tools keep it, with every value that is actually used still validated.
summary: Tools accept optional arguments that do not affect the requested operation instead of rejecting the call: `grep` treats an empty `include` as omitted, `update_goal` ignores fields its action does not use, `write` and `edit` allow a blank justification when no sandbox widening is requested, and `subagent` treats empty model fields as omitted.

reason: The two-chunk delivery comes from the Windows console layer, not from Node, so a Go pseudo-terminal sees it too. A default of zero keeps the behaviour opt-in; the terminal area should measure the right value again with its Go PTY library.
summary: The persistent terminal gains a `promptTailGraceMs` setting (default 0). After the prompt marker has been seen but its printable tail has not arrived, the readiness wait is extended by that amount, because the Windows pseudo-terminal delivers the marker and the prompt text in two chunks.

reason: The finding (the operating system's console host can be too old to render prompts reliably) stands, but the fix is a node-pty option. The Go design must choose a PTY library and decide whether to ship its own console host with it.
summary: On Windows, persistent terminals are allocated with the OpenConsole binary that the node-pty package ships (`useConptyDll: true`) instead of the console host of the operating system, because the system console host on one test machine did not render the prompt reliably.

reason: It stops a removed or renamed preset from breaking every new conversation in a workspace. Host-side verification under the write lease is language-neutral.
summary: `session.create` treats a named session id as a reuse candidate that the host verifies (no turn started, right directory, unarchived member of the workspace, no other writer). A reused blank session runs the requested preset, not the one its log recorded; a candidate that fails a check is left unchanged and a new session is created.

reason: Without logged facts an SDK consumer cannot reconstruct when background work actually ran. It follows the event-sourced session model the Go design keeps.
summary: Jobs owned by a session append `job/registered` and `job/settled` facts to the session log, with timestamps, owner, producer kind and a UUID job id that survives registry restarts. The settled fact says whether the producer reported completion or the bookkeeping was forced, and a failed journal append warns but never blocks cleanup.

reason: Cooperative yielding exists because Node runs host work on one thread. In Go the list is built on its own goroutine and the scheduler preempts it; the parts to keep are cancellation through the request context and never returning a partial list.
summary: Session-list assembly works against a monotonic deadline (`listWorkSliceMs`, default 16 ms) and yields to the event loop only when a slice is used up, so a large list does not monopolize the host and a small one pays no extra round trips. Cancellation is checked per row and no partial list is returned.

reason: The rule is about not misreporting job state from a launch acknowledgement, which any UI must honour. The Go host renders the card in a template from the same two facts (`background` and `running`); DH-ADR-3 changes only where it is rendered.
summary: The tool card of an explicit background `bash` or `pwsh` call shows the command and working directory in the ordinary shell layout. Once the launch is acknowledged the card becomes a static command display without a run-state dot or exit code, because the acknowledgement says nothing about the background job.

reason: Keeping the system prompt byte-stable across launches is a cost rule that holds for any host. The Go design should adopt the general rule (no per-process value in the system prompt); it has no earlier-format sessions to project.
summary: Two process-specific values, the implementation checkout path and the Web URL, move out of the system prompt into runtime context. The system prompt keeps only value-free guidance, so a different port or checkout no longer changes the prompt and misses the provider's prefix cache.

reason: The sentence was measured upstream to stop long sleep loops (about 25 minutes of sleeping in one recorded session). Prompt text is model-facing and carries over; the remark about re-rendering prompt snapshot files is upstream repository mechanics.
summary: The delegation guidance keeps the sentence that tells the model to end its turn when only waiting for subagent results remains, instead of sleeping or polling; a settled child delivers a notice that starts a new turn.

reason: It prevents a full prompt-cache miss after a compaction or prune, which is a direct token cost. It belongs with in-history system prompt replacement, which the Go design should keep.
summary: At the start of a new request series, the system-prompt projection rewrites the first message only when the effective prompt text must move. When the latest surviving system node already holds the rendering, the nodes stay where the cached history has them, so the provider's prefix cache still hits.

reason: Per-agent installation left a window in which the tools were missing and put them in a layer exempt from inherited restrictions. Inheritance through the context tree is how the Go cordis port scopes registrations.
summary: Each delegation tool instance registers its definition once, in the composition that owns it, and agents sharing a preset revision inherit it. A preset switch changes ancestry and needs no per-agent installation, and the tool schema lists preset ids without the candidates' descriptions.

reason: Real servers send malformed charset headers, and a strict decoder would reject readable pages. The rule is a small explicit heuristic that a Go decoder can apply the same way.
summary: When a response declares an unusable charset such as `utf-8,gbk`, the fetch provider looks for a UTF-8 label inside the declaration and, if one is present, decodes strictly as UTF-8; otherwise it fails before reading the body. Invalid UTF-8 is rejected, not guessed.

reason: The note records a benchmark run in which this sentence was the only change, and a session that read ranges with `sed` 60 times. Tool guidance is model-facing text and carries over word for word.
summary: The read tool's guidance names `cat`, `sed`, `head` and `tail` as the shell commands it replaces and says `offset` and `limit` read a line range, restoring wording that an unrelated revert had removed.

reason: The session is the authority for filesystem permission, and background inspection must not execute repository-configured helpers. Both are security rules for any host that runs Git.
summary: The change-request panel runs its Git queries under the session's own sandbox mode and subprocess provider instead of forcing read-only confinement. Command-local Git configuration disables clean and process filters, alongside the existing hook and external-diff restrictions, so inspection never runs code configured by the repository.

reason: The rule (an install failure must never show an empty details pane, and the dialog and the full log agree) stands. The installer itself changes: under DH-ADR-4 there is no pnpm run, so the diagnostics come from fetching and starting a plugin process.
summary: A failed plugin installation always shows the host's diagnostic in the dialog: a silent pnpm failure streams the diagnostic the host recorded, a failed GitHub connection check streams its command line (credentials removed), output and exit status, and the failure screen keeps the settled result as well as the live stream.

reason: This is pnpm deployment of the Node runtime that upstream embeds in its Python SDK. A Go host is one binary whose dependencies are pinned by `go.sum`, so there is no dependency tree to deploy.
summary: The Python package builder uses pnpm's default deployment, which derives a frozen production lockfile from the workspace lockfile, so the Node runtime bundled into the Python package has exactly the locked dependency versions.

reason: The requirement (a very large diff must not freeze the page or slow the rest of the application) stands, and the scoped-CSS finding applies to any HTML. The React memoization does not; the Go UI gets the same effect by rendering file sections on the host and loading them as they come into view.
summary: The changes view of a large change request (366 files in the measured case) stays responsive: CSS `:has()` rules are scoped to navigator rows, memoized file sections receive stable values, and an expanded file draws its lines only when it comes near the viewport.

reason: The goal (a draft's attachments survive a session switch) stands. Because images and files are already uploaded to the host when added, the Go design can keep the draft's attachment list on the host, which would also survive a reload.
summary: A composer draft that has attachments keeps its session's scope alive without an event connection, so switching sessions and back keeps the attachments, running uploads and retry state. After a page reload the composer says the attachments were discarded instead of restoring them.

reason: The mode cuts round trips and context use, and its design already puts the program in a separate sandboxed process, so the host language does not matter. The Go host keeps the seam and the control channel; a JavaScript runtime remains an external prerequisite for this mode.
summary: PTC (programmatic tool calling) is a presentation mode of the tool registry: instead of one schema per tool, the model gets a single `run_code` tool and a generated TypeScript declaration of the tools, and writes a program that calls them. Code execution is a capability seam (`ctx.ptcRuntime`) that knows nothing about tools, and the shipped runtime runs each program in a fresh Node process under the session's sandbox policy.

reason: One vocabulary for tool-policy asks and sandbox escalation, with fail-closed behaviour when nobody can answer, is a security property independent of language. A waterfall of listeners maps to an ordered handler chain in the Go cordis port.
summary: One service (`ctx.approval`) turns the question whether a specific action may proceed into a closed, one-shot outcome. Answerers are listeners registered by whoever owns a channel to a person, and with no answerer every request resolves `unavailable`, so the asking tool call is denied.

reason: Opt-in, per-call, fail-to-exclusive scheduling removes latency for independent reads without the scheduler having to prove anything. Goroutines make the parallel part simple; the order of log events must still be specified.
summary: Sibling tool calls in one assistant message may run in parallel when each tool's optional `isConcurrencySafe(args)` classifier returns exactly `true`. The classifier is synchronous, pure and looks only at its own call; anything else, including a classifier that throws or invalid arguments, makes the call exclusive.

reason: The depth cap is a safety bound worth keeping. The persona and tool-filter restore paths exist only to read historical upstream sessions, which DH-ADR-2 says the Go design need not do, so only the depth policy carries over.
summary: `maxDepth` is an absolute cap on how deep a delegation tree may grow, and a provider declares whether it can enforce it. Persona and tool-filter overrides are no longer accepted for new children (presets own composition) and survive only to restore children recorded in old sessions.

reason: Workflows whose state lives in a terminal (debuggers, REPLs, activated environments) need it, and it follows the capability-seam pattern the Go design keeps. The Go design needs its own PTY library choice.
summary: An optional capability family gives an agent persistent, line-oriented pseudo-terminal sessions that survive across tool calls, exposed through six `terminal_*` tools. A service defines the session contract and a backend runs a persistent shell with readiness detection and bounded buffers; full-screen applications and restoring a session after its process is lost are deferred.

reason: The compare-and-set contract and the authority rule (who may resume) prevent stale or unauthorized goal changes whatever the host language.
summary: Three exclusive tools, `get_goal`, `create_goal` and `update_goal`, let the model read, create and change a long-running goal in its own session. Updates are compare-and-set on goal id and revision, and resuming a paused goal is reserved for the user.

reason: Programs must not scrape ids out of prose. A canonical JSON output per tool is also what a Go tool returns naturally, and the declaration generator is a deterministic projection of schemas that the Go registry can produce.
summary: In PTC mode a tool binding resolves to the tool's final canonical JSON value, and a failed call rejects with a real `ToolCallError`, instead of every result being flattened to one string. The generated declaration gives each tool its real parameter and return types.

reason: Separating the durable conversation from the process-local residency removes a second queue and the coupling of background-task lifetime to conversation delivery. The model is about ownership and is language-neutral.
summary: A continuable subagent is one durable session with at most one live Activation (one period in which its reconstructed agent is resident in the process). The agent's own inbox is the only turn queue; an Activation may run several turns and stay resident while waiting for descendants, and its receipt owns the result and cancellation of that one residency.

reason: Peer addressing and a shared task board with protection against stale updates are needed for multi-agent work in any implementation.
summary: Every root session and its descendants form a Team identified by the root session id, with a durable compare-and-set task board. One package owns the durable semantics (`ctx.agentTeams`) and another the model-facing tools, whose results are compact JSON with declared schemas.

reason: It replaces a raw JSON dump with a readable row while keeping presentation out of the log. A semantic tag on the event is easy for a host template to switch on.
summary: A non-user message's source may declare a `form`, a small semantic vocabulary for the shape of the information (for example `instructions` read from workspace files, or a `catalog` of available items), separate from `kind`, which says who produced it. The UI chooses presentation from the form; colours and layout never enter the vocabulary.

reason: Windows needs a real confining executor, or shipped profiles fall back to full access. The mechanism is operating-system API calls that Go can make through its Windows system-call packages, and the reasoning about delete rights carries over unchanged.
summary: The Windows sandbox confines writes with a `WRITE_RESTRICTED` token whose restricting SIDs carry workspace and private-temp capabilities, lowered to Low integrity, with matching access-control entries and Low labels on the granted directories. It is built directly on raw Win32 ACL calls, not on mxc or AppContainer.

reason: Authority fixed by the operator and unreachable from the model is the point, and it is language-neutral. The Claude Code provider upstream uses an npm SDK; the Go provider has to drive the product another way, which the subagent area decides.
summary: The Claude Code and Codex subagent providers run unattended with a `permissionMode` fixed in the deployment profile, using each product's own mode names. The subagent tool schema carries no permission field, so a model or a single delegation cannot raise its own authority.

reason: Explicit, stable authorization of model routes prevents a silent growth of cost and capability when a provider or model appears.
summary: A host setting stores an `enabled` switch and an explicit list of exact `{ provider, model }` routes that a parent agent may choose for a child. Registering a new model adapter never widens the list, and each delegation call reads the current setting.

reason: Content-addressed storage with hard-linked names and receipt-based staging is host-side and language-neutral. The browser upload carriers become an ordinary HTTP upload from the Go UI.
summary: Non-image files are uploaded in the background through one FIFO queue as soon as they are picked, stored byte for byte with no type or size limit, and staged for the session under a receipt. Equal bytes are stored once under their digest, and each model-facing path is a read-only hard link to that object.

reason: Quoting stays a feature and the semantic draft snapshot is the right durable form. The editor is one of the JavaScript islands DH-ADR-3 allows, so the quote node is rebuilt inside that island and the React slot wiring around it goes away.
summary: A selected transcript excerpt becomes an atomic quote node in the composer's rich-text editor. Drafts persist quote text and spans in a semantic snapshot, not raw editor state, so they survive reload, session switches and failed sends.

reason: It is a product permission mode built on the tool pipeline's pre-execute gate, which the Go design keeps. Its stated limit (direct effects inside a program are not reviewed) must be carried over as a stated limit.
summary: An experimental `auto` permission mode runs with full access but has a reviewer model judge every tool call, including each tool call a program makes, before its body runs. There are no exemptions by tool name and no cached grants, and a denial never executes the body.

reason: Two processes appending to one log corrupt it, and only an arbiter outside every writer survives all failure modes. Go reaches the same kernel objects through system calls without a native add-on.
summary: A session's write handle holds a kernel lock for its whole life: `flock` on a lock file on POSIX and a named kernel semaphore on Windows. The kernel releases it when the holder dies, so a crashed writer never blocks a successor and no expiry bookkeeping exists; a live but stuck holder keeps the lock until its process exits.

reason: Runtime management of MCP servers with per-server status is a product requirement. MCP is also the protocol for tool-only plugins in DH-ADR-4, so this manager becomes more central in the Go design.
summary: A manager service owns the live-updatable list of MCP servers and reconciles a fleet of ordinary MCP client instances, so servers can be added, tested, enabled and removed from Settings at runtime. Plugins register servers as effects that end with the plugin, and the client owns connection supervision, status and startup budgets.

reason: Every prompt change otherwise costs the whole cached prefix in a long session. The capability is declared per model, so it is a provider fact and not a JavaScript one.
summary: For a model route that declares the capability, a changed system prompt is appended as a new system message later in the history instead of rewriting message 0, so the provider's prefix cache survives prompt changes such as entering plan mode or loading a skill.

reason: A shared side surface where features open tabs (preview, files, terminal, browser) stays a requirement. A drag-and-drop docking engine is client-side JavaScript; the UI area must decide between a small island for the layout and a simpler server-driven model of tabs and splits.
summary: The right column of the Web client is a per-session docking surface with split panes, tabs, floating panels and an undoable sequence of layout operations, into which plugins register tab types. It replaced a single-purpose detail panel.

reason: Flattening assistant history loses information that later tool turns need. The protocol mapping is provider behaviour and has to be implemented faithfully again in Go.
summary: The DeepSeek adapter speaks the Anthropic Messages protocol under one `deepseek-official` route, keeping thinking blocks, signatures, tool calls and cumulative usage as protocol fields instead of flattening them. A prepared call freezes endpoint, credential reference and model capabilities, so retries stay on one configuration.

reason: Declaring instead of copying avoids a second store and a second place to edit. It is a small host-side rule.
summary: The `present` tool declares existing workspace files as deliverables by path and optional description, without reading or copying them. The UI opens the current file in the host's default application; a moved or deleted file makes the declaration unavailable.

reason: Host-owned processes with views that can reattach fit the Go design, and the terminal is one of the JavaScript islands DH-ADR-3 names. Create that is idempotent on a caller-chosen id, and cleanup in the background, are worth keeping as written.
summary: A person can open interactive shells in the sidebar. The host owns each terminal by session and stays authoritative for process, title and screen contents; the browser renders with xterm.js, attaches with a bounded screen snapshot followed by ordered output, and a browser disconnect or tab switch leaves the process running.

reason: An isolated checkout per session is needed for parallel agent work, and running Git through the session's own subprocess and sandbox providers keeps one permission model.
summary: An experimental tool, `enter_worktree`, creates a named branch and checkout from a pinned local commit under `.agents/worktrees` and moves the session into it through the working-directory service. Creation never fetches, never copies uncommitted files and never widens the session's sandbox policy.

reason: DH-ADR-1 keeps experimental packages in scope. Because the page is rendered by the owner's host, a server-rendered UI should make the relay simpler than relaying a client application; the protocol itself may change under DH-ADR-2.
summary: An owner can share a running session through a Liveshare server that both sides can reach. The reader opens a link and sees the session rendered by the owner's own host with its plugins, limited to that session and the children the reader creates; access is by organization link plus a deployment allow-list.

reason: Agents on machines without development tools still need predictable interpreters. This is a payload for the agent's work, not a dependency of the host, so it applies to a Go desktop shell too; publishing a completed staged copy is the right failure behaviour.
summary: The desktop application ships Python, Node.js, pnpm and data-processing and Office libraries as one release-bound payload that a path-query tool installs into the harness home and reports by absolute path. It never changes `PATH` or package-manager configuration, and installation publishes a complete staged copy.

reason: Abandoned shells otherwise live forever, and killing on disconnect would lose running work. The policy is host-side and language-neutral.
summary: A browser terminal is reclaimed only after no window has held it and the host has confirmed it idle for two continuous hours. Running or unknown activity cancels the deadline, and a returning window reattaches the same process.

reason: The preview requirements stand (saved formula results, literal CSV strings, tolerance of unsupported drawings). Upstream parses in the browser to avoid the Office engine; the Go UI must choose between parsing on the host and rendering a table, or keeping a JavaScript island for the grid.
summary: Spreadsheets (XLSX, XLS, CSV, TSV) are previewed read-only in the browser with a JavaScript grid and parser libraries, showing each formula with its saved result. The host only serves bounded bytes, and a chart the viewer cannot draw must not block the cells.

reason: An iframe with a sandbox attribute is plain HTML, so the feature and its trust rules carry straight into a server-rendered page. The address rules are a security boundary and should be checked on the host.
summary: A `browser` sidebar tab shows a Web page in a sandboxed iframe. The address parser accepts only `http` and `https`, rejects embedded credentials, the application's own origin, `file:` and every other scheme, and chat links open in such a tab when the tab type is registered.

reason: Changes come from shells and editors as well as harness tools, so only operating-system watching is complete, and watching only what is open bounds the cost. The Go host needs a file-watching library in place of chokidar and pushes invalidations over its event stream.
summary: Sidebar previews and file trees refresh from on-demand operating-system file watches. A preview watches its file and the files it references; the tree watches only the direct entries of open directories and releases a watch on collapse. Watches carry invalidation only, and content is read again through the normal readers.

reason: It closes a real escape (deleting files outside the workspace) in the restricted-token sandbox. The fix is Windows security semantics and must be carried over exactly, with tests that try the escape.
summary: Each Windows sandbox grant applies three edits in one call: the capability allow entry, a deny of `FILE_DELETE_CHILD` for everyone on containers, and a Low integrity label, with the token lowered to Low. Together they stop a confined process deleting files outside its granted roots through the parent directory's delete right.

reason: A machine-readable configuration schema, and an exit code that says whether the document can replace native validation, are worth keeping. The approximations come from Schemastery's mutating validation and `!!js` expressions; Go configuration types can produce an exact schema, so the partial cases should disappear.
summary: `dsh --dump-config-schema` projects plugin configuration declarations to JSON Schema without mounting plugins. The command exits 1 whenever any part of the projection is approximate, disabled rows are inspected too, and where native validation would change its input the schema is widened instead of simulating the change.

reason: The desktop shell becomes a system webview hosted by Go, which has no Electron guest tag. The goal (a retained, navigable browser pane with per-workspace storage) needs a new mechanism or a recorded limit; this is an open question for the desktop area.
summary: On desktop the sidebar browser uses an Electron `<webview>` guest instead of an iframe, so it can show sites that refuse embedding and observe navigation. Pages stay alive across tab and layout changes, and storage partitions are keyed by workspace so related pages share sign-ins.

reason: The selection and inheritance semantics stand. The ordering marker exists only to stay compatible with historical logs; the Go session format can record the selection as an explicit field when the child is created.
summary: An explicit spawn preset resolves the currently registered definition; omitting it joins the parent's exact live composition. On restore, an independent selection is recognized by an `agent-preset/selected` event recorded before the child's first descriptor, a marker chosen so that the session format did not have to change.

reason: An archived session that keeps spending tokens out of sight is a product defect. Two extension events (ask, then stop) keep the workspace package free of feature knowledge and map to cordis events in Go.
summary: Archiving never hides running work. The workspace registry asks providers what still runs for a session and refuses to archive by default; with `stopActivity` it writes the archive and then asks the providers to stop. The registry itself knows no agent, job or schedule vocabulary.

reason: Answering from stored state closes the gap in which a session with no live agent could be archived while its reminders still fire. Ordering the delete behind creates that are still in flight is a concurrency rule Go must keep.
summary: The schedule provider answers archive admission from the stored task rows, not from a live agent, and a stop deletes those rows in one batch on the same serialized queue the tools use. An idle or cold session with armed reminders therefore refuses the archive.

reason: A person watching can overrule a misjudged denial without switching the whole session to full access, and failures stop being reported as refusals.
summary: When the session's approval policy is `ask`, an Auto review denial becomes a question to the person through the approval service instead of a final denial. A reviewer failure is reported as a failure, distinct from a denial, and the tool body does not run in either case.

reason: A debugging view of the session log stays useful. The upstream design navigates object graphs held in the browser, which the Go UI does not have; the host can render the same grouping directly from the log, a page at a time.
summary: An experimental sidebar page shows a session's raw log, chat structures and rendered conversation side by side in a virtual table grouped by turn, step and event. It adds no stream or storage and reads data that the session controller and chat already hold in the browser.

reason: Multi-file edits in one guarded call are cheaper for the model and keep mutation intents visible for review. Preflight before commit, and the stated outcome of a half-finished move (`sourceDeleted`), are the failure semantics to keep.
summary: `apply_patch` accepts one Codex-style patch that adds, updates, deletes and moves several files. A pure library parses and matches it, the filesystem service gains `patchText`, `deleteFile` and `moveFile` with intent events and version guards, and a whole-patch preflight commits nothing if any part is refused.

reason: The safe-reader rules (only configured URLs, no redirects, bounded size) carry over. What an entry installs changes under DH-ADR-4 from an npm bundle to a plugin process package, so the path from an entry to installation is redesigned.
summary: An experimental, off-by-default bundle adds a host service that reads plugin market indexes and a Discover tab that lists their entries. Index sources are user data; the host fetches only configured URLs, refuses redirects, bounds the body and never writes the profile.

reason: One self-contained index document that third parties can publish is a good shape. Its identity fields are npm's; Go plugins are processes or MCP servers (DH-ADR-4) and the Go design need not keep the file format (DH-ADR-2), so the index needs identity and version fields of its own.
summary: A market is one JSON index document, kept separate from whatever generates it. The format reuses npm package names, versions, ranges, distribution tags and person declarations, and adds localized titles, categories and labels.

reason: One hosted server can cost over 200,000 characters of tool definitions on every request; loading on demand removes that cost without a new event type. Agent-scoped registration released on disposal is the cordis model.
summary: An MCP server marked `toolLoading: on-demand` keeps its tools out of the registry. The model sees one loader tool per server and a catalog of tool names with the first line of each description in the system prompt, and loaded tools register in a scope owned by that agent.

reason: A host half that assembles one streamed state per session is already the shape a server-rendered panel fed by server-sent events needs. The React half is expressed again as templates under DH-ADR-3.
summary: An experimental two-part feature shows a session's change requests with checks, reviews and mergeability, and offers sessions that work in their own worktree. The host half assembles everything the panel shows into one streamed state, and one default-disabled Plugins entry enables the whole code-change workflow.

reason: Deriving bindings from the log keeps one source of truth, and leaving forge credentials in the vendor tool's own store is a security choice. Both are language-neutral.
summary: Change requests are bound to a session by a projection over its log: it reads `gh pr create`, `gh pr view` and `git push` calls and their results, so no separate store exists and bindings survive fork and resume. A provider-neutral registry shares polling, and the GitHub provider reads through the GitHub CLI on the host, so credentials never enter the session's execution environment.

reason: It unifies two terminal systems behind one controller and gives a clear rule for handing control over. Telling typed input apart from terminal-protocol replies stays a concern of the terminal island.
summary: An experimental backend makes the agent's persistent terminals ordinary sidebar terminals that a person can watch. A terminal records who opened it; the person's first typed input takes control, after which agent writes, signals and closing are refused while reads continue.

reason: Install icons and the manifest are static files that the Go host serves unchanged. The icon rendering script is upstream build tooling and is not carried over as such.
summary: The Web app's install manifest carries four icons rendered from the official application tile (192 and 512 pixel, a maskable 512 pixel and a 180 pixel Apple touch icon) and requests `standalone` display in place of `fullscreen`. A browser test measures the maskable icon's safe area.

reason: A page left open across a host upgrade still happens with server-rendered HTML, because the scripts and styles it loaded belong to the old release. The Go UI has no module graph to hot-replace, so the mechanism reduces to comparing a release identity on reconnect and prompting for a reload.
summary: A release is the host's version plus an optional source commit. A page applies hot module updates only while the connected host serves the release the page booted from; when the release differs, nothing is applied and a dialog asks the user to reload.

reason: It is a reading rule about what a user must not lose, independent of the rendering technology. The host template applies it and the setting stays in host settings; DH-ADR-3 changes only where it is rendered.
summary: When a finished turn folds, every assistant reply stays visible and only the process (tool calls, reasoning) folds. A general setting, `ui-chat.foldedReplies`, can restore the old rule of showing only the final answer.

reason: It removes a wasted generation per search and fits the web capability seam, in which providers are swappable behind fixed tool schemas.
summary: DeepSeek's dedicated Search and Fetch APIs are implemented as providers behind the existing `web_search` and `web_fetch` tools, registered as `deepseek-search-api` and `deepseek-fetch-api` and selected independently. Retrieval no longer needs an auxiliary model request per query.

reason: A detail page with a deterministic, localized fallback order is worth keeping. The lookup is defined over npm package layout and locale JSON files; under DH-ADR-4 a plugin is a process package with its own manifest, so the order is stated again over that manifest.
summary: A plugin's long description is read in a fixed order: the Markdown file named by `meta.detail` in the package's locale file for the display language, then shorter language prefixes, then English, then the package README, and for a market entry the README of its repository directory.

reason: Authority by recorded source, not by message role, is the rule that makes a model reviewer safe against injected text. It is language-neutral.
summary: Auto review can be selected explicitly in headless, SDK and ACP hosts. Text whose recorded source is the user counts as instruction whether a human or a supervising program sent it; files, tool results and injected context never gain instruction authority, and task text cannot choose its own source.

reason: An out-of-process host must be able to answer questions, or the tool has no answerer. The Python SDK is in scope (DH-ADR-1); the wire details may change (DH-ADR-2), but the capability handshake and the cancellation rules should stay.
summary: SDK clients (TypeScript and Python) may register a question callback and advertise it at initialization. The SDK server then routes the `ask_user_question` interaction to the client over a bidirectional call for the root agents it owns, validates a complete batch of answers and cancels pending questions when the tool or server stops.

reason: It is a display rule fed by host projections, which a server-rendered list can read directly; DH-ADR-3 changes only the rendering.
summary: Each session-list row shows a branch glyph while the session works in its own worktree, and the glyph of its most urgent change request, with a hover card naming the branch and up to three change requests. The facts reach the list as cached projection views, so sessions that are not loaded show them too.

reason: Sending a message no longer carries megabytes of base64 in one call, and validation errors appear when the image is added. Receipt-based staging is host-side and suits an HTML upload.
summary: The composer uploads each image as soon as it is added, through the same background queue as files. The host validates, normalizes and stores it and returns a receipt; the prompt cites the receipt, and stored images count toward the per-message limits.

reason: The rule matters only if the Go UI keeps floating panels (see the docking note). If it does, the constraint that a floating panel can always be recovered lives inside that JavaScript island; if it does not, there is nothing to carry.
summary: Floating dock panels may be dragged past the viewport edge but spring back into a legal region when released, so a panel's header and resize corner can never be lost off screen. The rule lives in one shared gesture hook.

reason: Changing a release marker should not need a client release, and the listing is an external service contract that the Go adapter reads the same way. Validation of the text happens on the host.
summary: A model's badge in the selector (text and tone) comes from the service's `/models` listing, under the `deepseek-harness` key of `client_metadata`, not from a client package that matches model names. The text is limited to 1 to 12 visible characters on one line, and control characters are rejected.

reason: The state already lives on the host, which is where a server-rendered UI wants it. The area should decide whether in-memory is still enough, because the records are lost when the host restarts.
summary: The host keeps one reading record per session in memory and streams it to every client, so unread-completion and failure marks agree across browsers, including for turns that end while no client is connected. Reading activity never enters the session log or the model's history.

reason: Reusing ordinary message admission avoids a special loop branch and a new durable event, and no artificial instruction enters the history.
summary: After an eligible model failure, a play action submits an empty prompt whose source is `retry`. The ordinary admission path records an empty user message and opens a new balanced turn, and the failed turn stays closed. A fixed allowlist of six failure codes decides eligibility.

reason: Adopt. The Go design lays out its home directory from scratch (DH-ADR-2), so it can start with categories and one resolver at no migration cost; the categories tell an operator what is safe to delete and what must be backed up.
summary: Proposal, not finished upstream: group every path under the harness home directory into `config`, `data`, `state`, `cache` and `backup` categories modelled on the XDG Base Directory Specification, all still inside the home, with one path helper that every package uses. Well-known top-level entries such as `.env` and `sessions/` keep their places.

reason: Do not adopt. The plan migrates React client code that DH-ADR-3 replaces; a server-rendered page reads host configuration when it renders, so there is nothing to migrate. The inventory remains useful as a list of UI features that depend on host configuration.
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: an inventory of packages whose browser half reads host configuration by its own means (page globals, the settings mirror) and a plan to move each of them to browser configuration sync.

reason: Adopt. It gives one vocabulary for native tools, program-only tools and on-demand loading, and the Go tool registry can be designed around it from the start instead of having it added later.
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: describe every tool by two model-facing dimensions, reachability (`native`, `program` or `both`) and initial disclosure (`none`, `name`, `summary` or `full`), in place of the single provider-specific `deferLoading` flag. Every reachable tool stays searchable.

reason: Adopt. Without it one lost file makes a session permanently unusable; recording the quarantine as an event keeps requests reconstructable from the log.
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: when an image attachment in the history is missing, corrupt or unreadable, append an `attachment/quarantine` event so that later requests leave that image out, instead of every later model request failing on the same object.

reason: Adopt the constraint and defer the feature. The Go loop can place a rewrite phase before the log commit from the start, which upstream cannot do without reordering events; the open question of whether providers accept a rewritten assistant message on replay must be settled first.
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: let a pre-tool hook rewrite a tool call's arguments as a transaction that runs before the call's identity is created, so that the audit event (with the original kept beside it), the derived model history and the UI all show what actually ran. Mutating the frozen execution object is ruled out.

reason: Adopt as later-priority scope. It needs only what the event-sourced log already provides, keeps the request prefix cache-stable across compactions and makes compaction recoverable for the model; it is not required for a first working compaction.
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: split compaction output into frozen index checkpoints that are never rewritten and one mutable state checkpoint, and give the model `history_read` and `history_search` tools to read compacted spans back from the session log.

reason: Adopt as deferred scope. It composes primitives the Go design already keeps (session fork, agent attach, injected context) and needs no new mechanism, but upstream has not built or validated it, so it should not be in the first stages.
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: a side session is an ordinary live session forked at the source's last completed turn and framed as a read-only advisor, which the user talks to separately and which can merge one condensed note back into the parent.

reason: Adopt the idea with a different renderer. A bounded declarative model is easier to serve from a Go host than from a client plugin: the host validates the description and renders it with templates, which DH-ADR-3 already requires.
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: Task Surface, a versioned declarative description of a temporary structured interaction (compare options, reorder a plan, fill related fields) that an agent emits for one tool call. The product validates, places and renders it and returns the user's conclusion; no generated code runs.

reason: Adopt if the Go desktop application keeps the same business server: the endpoint is an external service contract and does not depend on the shell technology. The desktop area must confirm the service exists before making it a deliverable.
summary: Proposal, backend integration in progress upstream: a guest-accessible endpoint, `GET /api/v0/check_client_update`, tells the desktop application whether its version must be updated before use, with explicit success, blocking and error semantics, kept separate from the choice of update artifacts.

reason: Keep the decision as upstream made it, which is to defer: none of the candidates is built or approved, and each adds installer states. They are recorded so that the Go update design does not rule them out, for example by keeping full SemVer comparison.
summary: Proposal, explicitly deferred upstream: possible later desktop update features (independently revised desktop packages with a `.dsk.N` version suffix, a stable channel, installation on next launch, replacing a pending update), none of them a requirement of the first update flow.

reason: Adopt the policy (discover automatically, download and restart only with approval, never interrupt running tasks silently). The installer mechanism upstream belongs to the Electron application; the Go desktop shell under DH-ADR-3 needs its own verified update mechanism.
summary: Proposal recording the outstanding release and backend work for desktop updates: automatic discovery, user-initiated download, visible preparation state and a separate restart approval that accounts for running tasks, with signed Windows and macOS upgrades qualified end to end.

reason: Do not adopt. The bridge depends on importing TypeScript into the host process with the host's full authority and on in-process hooks, which DH-ADR-4 rules out. A Node side process could host such extensions over the plugin protocol, but upstream has not built the bridge and nothing in the Go design depends on it.
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: an experimental bridge that loads unmodified Pi coding-agent extension sources (TypeScript factories) into the host process and serves Pi's extension API from existing extension points, as a capability demonstration.

reason: The decision to build nothing holds in Go, and more strongly: every higher level runs a JavaScript composition runtime in or beside the host, which DH-ADR-4 would turn into a separate process. Nothing is carried over except the watch on Pi's release status.
summary: Proposal that recommends building nothing now: Pi's newer plugin mechanism is unpublished and unstable, so compatibility is described as six levels, each tied to an upstream trigger, and the product stays at level 0 (no support).
